public_rationale: The sentence describes Bjarnason's essay and endorses its theory. The essay does set out a six-step 'LLMentalist Effect' that it compares with a psychic's con. One step, for example, says chatbot answers sound specific to the context but are statistically generic (e1). The endorsed theory says an 'unthinking' LLM 'cons many of its users' without meaning to. The claim gives no measure of being 'conned' and no threshold for 'many', and 'unthinking' is a contested label. A sycophancy study reports that five AI assistants consistently gave answers matching user beliefs across four text-generation tasks (e2). That is related to the essay's idea of validation. But it does not measure how many users are misled about LLM abilities, or whether a cold-reading-like process is the cause. The claim cannot be scored as true or false.
limitations: The essay page shows no publication date. Its date is recorded as 2023 based on Marcus's note ('from last year'), and its available_at is the post date.
e1 is an opinion essay. It shows what the essay argues, not that users are actually misled.
The cited version of e2 is dated 10 May 2025, after the post. The study's first version is dated 20 October 2023.
No source in the packet measures what share of users are misled about LLM abilities.
The description of the essay's content was not graded separately.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: An unthinking LLM, without meaning to do so, cons many of its users through a process that closely parallels a psychic's con.

statement.excerpt: The second summary, deeply parallel with the first, outlines the process by which an unthinking LLM (without meaning to do so) cons many of its users.
statement.document_title: LLMs aren’t very bright. Why are so many people fooled?

from_speaker: "deeply parallel with the first" (the psychic's con)
our_interpretation: Part of the sentence just describes Bjarnason's essay. The essay does set out a six-step 'LLMentalist Effect' that mirrors its six-step 'psychic's con'. That description is accurate, but it is not a claim about the world.

The substantive part is that LLMs 'con many of its users' through a mechanism like cold reading. That is an interpretive theory with no stated measure: what counts as being 'conned', how many is 'many', and how the mechanism would be shown. 'Unthinking' is also a contested philosophical label.
Related research on sycophancy (models telling users what they want to hear) is relevant context. It does not test the cold-reading 'con' theory or how many users are misled.
criteria.support_condition: Would need studies that measure what share of users are misled about LLM abilities and show this happens through cold-reading-style validation. The claim sets no threshold, so this is not scorable.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Would need studies showing users are generally not misled, or are misled by mechanisms unlike cold reading. No threshold is stated, so this is not scorable.
